extracted.intended_audience: engineers preparing invention disclosures and working with patent attorneys (inventors/engineers at startups & product teams)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for engineers on preparing invention disclosures and interacting with patent attorneys to produce broad, defensible patent specifications and claims. Emphasizes what technical information, variants, and behaviours matter for patentability and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bring an Invention Disclosure, Not a Marketing Doc
rubrics_metrics.description: A useful invention disclosure has: (1) the technical problem in operational terms, (2) the closest known prior solution and why it falls short, (3) the new solution explained as if to a competent engineer who has not seen it, (4) at least one alternative way to implement the new solution, and (5) the result data if you have any. Marketing language ("disrupts," "revolutionary," "best-in-class") is filler.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete technical details rather than marketing claims. Include the operational problem and the closest prior art plus shortcomings, a clear engineer-level explanation of your solution, implementation alternatives, and any experimental or result data. Avoid vague, promotional phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Difference Between a Feature and an Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: A feature is something a user notices. An invention is a non-obvious technical mechanism that achieves a feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing your work, focus on mechanisms, not user-facing features. Example: 'Push notifications when the package arrives' is a feature; 'A geofence-triggered notification scheduler that batches push events to reduce radio wakeups' is closer to an invention you can claim. Translate features into their enabling technical mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whiteboards Are Better Than Slides
rubrics_metrics.description: When you meet with the attorney, sketch on a whiteboard. Slides force you to commit to one architecture; whiteboards let you say 'or alternatively...' which is exactly what your attorney needs to write a broad spec.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use sketching to show multiple architectures and alternatives instead of polished slide decks. Emphasize alternative flows/implementations verbally and visually so the attorney can capture breadth and fallback options for claims; avoid presenting only a single committed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the 'Inventive Concept' in One Sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: If you cannot finish the sentence 'The new thing is that ____,' you do not yet have an invention you can claim. The blank should be filled with a mechanism, not a goal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distill the invention into a single-sentence mechanism statement to test claimability. Ensure the sentence describes how something is done (a mechanism), not merely what outcome is achieved or a marketing goal. Use this as a gate before investing in drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants Matter More Than the Best Mode
rubrics_metrics.description: The single best version of your invention is what your competitors will design around. Your attorney needs to know the worse versions, the ugly hacks, the alternative materials. Each one becomes a fallback claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document multiple implementations, degraded or cheaper variants, and hacked/ugly solutions. Provide alternative materials and less-preferred embodiments so the attorney can draft broader and multiple fallback claims to prevent easy design-arounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art You Already Know
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell your attorney every prior solution you considered. This is not an admission of unpatentability - it is the foundation for distinguishing your work. The duty of disclosure (Rule 56) requires you to disclose what you know is material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be comprehensive and candid about known prior solutions and references you encountered. Providing this information helps craft distinguishing arguments and satisfies disclosure duties; withholding known material prior art is harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer 'Why Did Nobody Do This Before' for Non-Obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If a colleague asks 'why didn't anyone do this before,' your answers are worth gold: a technical bias was misleading the field; an enabling component just became affordable; a counter-intuitive trade-off had to be accepted. Write these down. They become the heart of the 103 non-obviousness argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record economic, technical, and historical reasons that made the invention non-obvious. Explain biases, enabling events, cost changes, or accepted trade-offs that your invention overcomes — these points support the inventive-step (35 U.S.C. §103) argument in prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Publish, Demo, or Sell Before Filing
rubrics_metrics.description: In the U.S. you have a one-year grace period (35 USC 102(b)(1)) but most other countries have absolute novelty. A conference talk, a sales pitch with a non-NDA prospect, or a public demo on the same day as filing can kill your foreign rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid public disclosures (talks, demos, unprotected sales pitches) before filing if you intend to obtain foreign patents. If disclosure is unavoidable, consult counsel about filing first or using confidentiality agreements; do not rely on U.S.-only grace periods for global protection.
